title: Οἱ ἱκέται
about: The herdsman finishes his taunt over Ctesippus, and Odysseus and Telemachus strike down two more suitors. Athena shows her aegis from the roof, and the suitors scatter like cattle stung by a gadfly while the four fall on them like vultures on small birds. Leiodes, the suitors’ sacrificing priest, clasps Odysseus’s knees and swears he did no wrong; Odysseus answers that a man who prayed for his homecoming to fail has earned his death, and kills him. Phemius the minstrel, torn between the altar of Zeus and the knees of Odysseus, begs for his life, and Telemachus asks his father to spare him and the herald Medon, who lies hidden under a chair in an oxhide. Odysseus sends the two to wait in the courtyard, looks over the hall, where the suitors lie like fish on the sand, and tells Telemachus to call the nurse Eurycleia.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα βοῶν ἑλίκων ἐπιβουκόλος·
sentences.l: He spoke, the herdsman of the crumple-horned cattle;
sentences.i: So spoke the herdsman of the cattle with crumpled horns.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα is 'so he said', the closing formula for a speech; here it ends the herdsman’s speech over Ctesippus, which stood at the end of the previous part. ἦ is a form of ἠμί 'say' and ῥα is the particle ἄρα. βοῶν ἑλίκων ἐπιβουκόλος is 'the herdsman of the crumple-horned cattle': ἑλίκων is the genitive plural of ἕλιξ 'twisted, curved', the adjective of the epithet ἕλικες βόες, and ἐπιβουκόλος is the standing description of the man who tends the cattle. The ano teleia after ἐπιβουκόλος closes the clause in mid-line, so this unit is half a line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
οὖτα Δαμαστορίδην αὐτοσχεδὸν ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ.
sentences.l:
and Odysseus
stabbed Damastor’s son at close quarters with a long spear.
sentences.i: and Odysseus stabbed the son of Damastor at close quarters with his long spear.
sentences.n: Δαμαστορίδην is the patronymic 'son of Damastor' standing for the man himself: it is Agelaus, who is named in the previous part and again in line 327. αὐτάρ is 'and, but', and οὖτα is a past tense of οὐτάω 'wound with a thrust', with no augment. αὐτοσχεδόν is 'at close quarters, hand to hand' (αὐτός with the root of σχεδόν 'near'), and ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is 'with a long spear', the dative of instrument, ἔγχεϊ being the epic dative of ἔγχος.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ Εὐηνορίδην Λειώκριτον οὖτα
δουρὶ μέσον κενεῶνα, διαπρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσεν·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus Evenor’s son Leiocritus stabbed
with a spear in the middle of the flank, and right through the bronze he drove;
sentences.i: Telemachus stabbed Leiocritus, son of Evenor, with his spear in the middle of the flank, and drove the bronze clean through.
sentences.n: οὖτα ends this line as it ended the one before, 'stabbed' again, with Telemachus now the subject. Εὐηνορίδην is the patronymic 'son of Evenor', in apposition to Λειώκριτον. δουρί is the dative of δόρυ 'spear' (the epic form), and κενεών is the 'flank', the soft hollow of the side below the ribs; μέσον κενεῶνα 'in the middle of the flank' puts the place struck in the accusative. διαπρό 'right through' goes with ἔλασσεν, the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive', which has a doubled σ and no augment; χαλκόν 'bronze' is the spearhead.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δὲ πρηνής, χθόνα δ’ ἤλασε παντὶ μετώπῳ.
sentences.l: And he fell face down, and the ground he struck with his whole forehead.
sentences.i: He fell on his face and struck the ground with his whole forehead.
sentences.n: The subject is Leiocritus, not repeated. ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω 'fall headlong, crash down', and πρηνής 'face down' is nominative, agreeing with him. χθόνα is the poetic word for 'ground', and ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'strike', the same verb as ἔλασσεν in the line before. παντὶ μετώπῳ is 'with his whole forehead', a dative of instrument.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ Ἀθηναίη φθισίμβροτον αἰγίδ’ ἀνέσχεν
ὑψόθεν ἐξ ὀροφῆς·
sentences.l:
Then indeed Athena the mortal-destroying aegis held up
from on high, out of the roof;
sentences.i: Then Athena held up her mortal-destroying aegis from on high, out of the roof;
sentences.n: In the previous part Athena has perched in the rafters in the shape of a swallow; now she shows herself with the aegis, the terrifying emblem of Zeus and Athena. The poem does not say here what it looks like, and the name is traditionally connected with αἴξ 'goat'. αἰγίδ’ is the accusative singular, the final -α elided. φθισίμβροτον is a compound of φθίω 'perish, waste' (here causative, 'destroy') and βροτός 'mortal', the house 'mortal-destroying'. ἀνέσχεν is the aorist of ἀνέχω 'hold up'. ὑψόθεν is 'from on high', with the suffix -θεν of 'from', and ἐξ ὀροφῆς 'out of the roof'. The ano teleia after ὀροφῆς closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: τῶν δὲ φρένες ἐπτοίηθεν.
sentences.l: and of them the wits were terrified.
sentences.i: and their wits were thrown into a panic.
sentences.n: τῶν is 'of them', the suitors, and φρένες 'wits' is the mind as the seat of thought, not the body-part sense 'midriff'. ἐπτοίηθεν is the aorist passive of πτοιέω 'terrify, throw into a flutter'; the ending -θεν stands for -θησαν, an epic form of the third person plural.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐφέβοντο κατὰ μέγαρον βόες ὣς ἀγελαῖαι·
sentences.l: And they fled through the hall, like cows of the herd;
sentences.i: They fled in panic through the hall like cows of the herd;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is 'and they', the suitors again, and ἐφέβοντο is the imperfect of φέβομαι 'flee in terror'. κατὰ μέγαρον is 'through the hall'. βόες ὣς ἀγελαῖαι is 'like cows of the herd': ὣς with a circumflex stands after its noun and works as 'like', and ἀγελαῖαι is the adjective from ἀγέλη 'herd'. This begins a simile of cattle that fills the rest of this line and the next two; a second simile, of vultures, follows it.

sentences.t:
τὰς μέν τ’ αἰόλος οἶστρος ἐφορμηθεὶς ἐδόνησεν
ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ, ὅτε τ’ ἤματα μακρὰ πέλονται.
sentences.l:
them indeed the darting gadfly, having rushed upon them, drove wild
in the season of spring, when the days are long.
sentences.i: A darting gadfly falls on such cows and drives them wild, in the spring season, when the days are long.
sentences.n: τὰς is 'them', the cows. μέν τε are the particle μέν with epic τε, which marks a thing that happens every time, and ἐδόνησεν is the aorist of δονέω 'shake, drive to frenzy' in that general sense, so the English can use the present. αἰόλος 'darting' also means 'gleaming, dappled'; the picture here is the quick swerving of the gadfly, but the poem does not decide between the senses. οἶστρος is the 'gadfly', and ἐφορμηθείς the aorist passive participle of ἐφορμάω 'rush upon'. Line 301 is word for word a line already published, and keeps its English: ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ 'in the season of spring' and ὅτε τ’ ἤματα μακρὰ πέλονται 'when the days are long', ἤματα being the plural of ἦμαρ.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὥς τ’ αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες ἀγκυλοχεῖλαι,
ἐξ ὀρέων ἐλθόντες ἐπ’ ὀρνίθεσσι θόρωσι·
sentences.l:
and they, like vultures, crook-taloned, hook-beaked,
out of the mountains having come, upon birds leap;
sentences.i: And they were like hook-taloned, hook-beaked vultures that have come down from the mountains and leap on birds;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is 'and they', now the attackers, set against the cattle of the simile just given; the verb 'were' is left out. ὥς τε is 'just as', and the birds are αἰγυπιοί, a word for a large bird of prey, 'vulture' by tradition, the exact species not known. γαμψώνυχες 'crook-taloned' is γαμψός 'curved' with ὄνυξ 'claw', and ἀγκυλοχεῖλαι 'hook-beaked' is ἀγκύλος 'hooked' with χεῖλος 'lip', here the beak. ἐξ ὀρέων is 'out of the mountains', the uncontracted genitive plural of ὄρος, and ὀρνίθεσσι the dative plural of ὄρνις 'bird'. θόρωσι is the aorist subjunctive of θρῴσκω 'leap', with no κε, as in a general simile.

sentences.t:
ταὶ μέν τ’ ἐν πεδίῳ νέφεα πτώσσουσαι ἵενται,
οἱ δέ τε τὰς ὀλέκουσιν ἐπάλμενοι, οὐδέ τις ἀλκὴ
γίγνεται οὐδὲ φυγή·
sentences.i: The birds dart across the plain, cowering beneath the clouds, while the vultures leap on them and destroy them, and the birds have no might to resist, and no escape in flight;
sentences.n: ταί is 'those', the birds, and οἱ δέ τε 'and these', the vultures, with epic τε. ἵενται is the third person plural of ἵεμαι 'dart, rush'. The construction of νέφεα πτώσσουσαι is not clear: πτώσσω is 'cower, shrink', and the accusative νέφεα 'clouds' can be taken as what they cower before, towards or under; the translation keeps to 'cowering beneath the clouds' and does not claim more. ὀλέκουσιν is 'destroy', ἐπάλμενοι the syncopated aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι 'leap upon', and ἀλκή is 'might', the house word, here the strength to resist. The ano teleia after φυγή closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: χαίρουσι δέ τ’ ἀνέρες ἄγρῃ·
sentences.l: and rejoice, men, in the hunt;
sentences.i: and men take delight in the hunt;
sentences.n: ἀνέρες is the old form of ἄνδρες 'men', and χαίρω takes the dative: ἄγρῃ is 'the hunt, the catch'. The line brings in the human watcher of the scene: men take pleasure in such a hunt. δέ τε is again the epic τε of what always happens.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τοὶ μνηστῆρας ἐπεσσύμενοι κατὰ δῶμα
τύπτον ἐπιστροφάδην·
sentences.l:
So then those, upon the suitors rushing through the house,
were striking, turning from one to another;
sentences.i: So the four of them rushed at the suitors through the house and struck them down, wheeling from one man to the next;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα 'so then' brings the poem back from the simile to the fight. τοί is the article as a pronoun, 'they': Odysseus, Telemachus and the two herdsmen. ἐπεσσύμενοι is the participle of ἐπισεύομαι 'rush at', with the doubled σ, and κατὰ δῶμα is 'through the house'. τύπτον is the imperfect of τύπτω 'strike'. ἐπιστροφάδην is an adverb in -δην from ἐπιστρέφω 'turn upon': they turn from one man to another. The ano teleia after it closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ στόνος ὤρνυτ’ ἀεικὴς
κράτων τυπτομένων, δάπεδον δ’ ἅπαν αἵματι θῦε.
sentences.l:
and of them a groaning rose, unseemly,
of heads being struck, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.i: and an unseemly groaning rose from their stricken heads, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.n: τῶν is 'of them', the suitors; στόνος is 'groaning', and ὤρνυτ’ the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι, 'rose', with elision. ἀεικής 'unseemly' agrees with στόνος, and is the word of the house ἀεικέα πότμον. κράτων is the genitive plural of κάρ 'head', and κράτων τυπτομένων is 'of heads being struck'. The last clause, δάπεδον δ’ ἅπαν αἵματι θῦε 'the whole floor seethed with blood', has the words of 11.420 and keeps their English; θῦε is the imperfect of θύω 'rush, seethe' without augment.

sentences.t:
Λειώδης δ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἐπεσσύμενος λάβε γούνων,
καί μιν λισσόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And Leiodes, rushing forward, took hold of Odysseus’s knees,
and him, entreating, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And Leiodes rushed forward and took hold of Odysseus’s knees, and, entreating him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Leiodes is the suitors’ sacrificing priest, as he says of himself at 318. To take a man by the knees is the suppliant’s gesture: λάβε γούνων has the genitive of the part taken hold of, and Ὀδυσῆος is the possessor, 'of Odysseus’. ἐπεσσύμενος is 'rushing forward', and λισσόμενος the participle of λίσσομαι 'entreat'. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα 'spoke winged words' is the house rendering. The ano teleia after προσηύδα introduces the speech.

sentences.t: γουνοῦμαί σ’, Ὀδυσεῦ·
sentences.l: “I beseech you at your knees, Odysseus;
sentences.i: “I entreat you, Odysseus;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Leiodes speaks. γουνοῦμαι is 'I beseech at the knees', built on γόνυ 'knee' and the verb of the suppliant’s gesture just made; the house has 'I beseech you at your knees' in the long layer and 'I entreat you' in the short one. σ’ is σε, and Ὀδυσεῦ the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς, written with one σ here as often. The ano teleia closes a very short unit.

sentences.t: σὺ δέ μ’ αἴδεο καί μ’ ἐλέησον·
sentences.l: and you, revere me, and pity me;
sentences.i: and you, show me respect and take pity on me;
sentences.n: σὺ δέ is 'and you', set against the violence round them. αἴδεο is the imperative of αἰδέομαι 'have regard for, show respect to', the ending -εο standing for Attic -ου; it is the verb of the claim a suppliant has on the man he kneels to. ἐλέησον is the aorist imperative of ἐλεέω 'pity, take pity on'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τινά φημι γυναικῶν ἐν μεγάροισιν
εἰπεῖν οὐδέ τι ῥέξαι ἀτάσθαλον·
sentences.l:
For never yet, I say, to any of the women in the halls
have I said or done any wanton thing;
sentences.i: For I tell you that I have never yet said or done anything wanton to any of the women in the halls;
sentences.n: Leiodes begins his defence. οὐ γάρ πώ ... φημι is 'for I say that not yet', and the infinitives εἰπεῖν and ῥέξαι, both aorist, say what he claims never to have done: οὐ ... φημι puts the negative on them. τινὰ γυναικῶν is 'any one of the women', with the partitive genitive, and is the person who suffers the word or deed. ἀτάσθαλον is the neuter adjective used as a noun, 'a wanton thing', from the same root as ἀτασθαλίαι 'wanton follies'. The ano teleia after it closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους
παύεσκον μνηστῆρας, ὅτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι.
sentences.l:
but also others
I used to stop, suitors, whoever should do such things.
sentences.i: and I used to stop other suitors too, any who did such things.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους is 'but also others', and μνηστῆρας stands in apposition to it. παύεσκον is the imperfect of παύω with the iterative suffix -σκ-, 'used to stop', and has no augment. ὅτις is ὅς τις 'whoever', and ῥέζοι the present optative of ῥέζω 'do', the optative of a general past case: whoever it was who did such things. τοιαῦτά γε is 'such things, at least'.

sentences.t: ἀλλά μοι οὐ πείθοντο κακῶν ἄπο χεῖρας ἔχεσθαι·
sentences.l: But to me they did not obey, from evils to keep their hands off;
sentences.i: but they would not obey me and keep their hands from evil;
sentences.n: ἀλλά 'but' gives the other side of what he has just said. πείθοντο is the imperfect middle of πείθω, 'were obeying', with the dative μοι 'me', and οὐ makes it 'would not'. κακῶν ἄπο is ἀπὸ κακῶν 'from evils', the preposition after its noun with the accent on the first syllable. χεῖρας ἔχεσθαι is 'to keep their hands', the middle infinitive of ἔχω with ἀπό in the sense 'hold off from'.

sentences.t: τῷ καὶ ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐπέσπον.
sentences.l: Therefore too, by their wanton-follies, an unseemly doom they met.
sentences.i: That is why, through their wanton folly, they met an unseemly doom.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore', an old dative of the article used as an adverb; do not confuse it with τῷ 'with it'. καί here is 'too, indeed'. ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is the dative plural in -ῃσιν of ἀτασθαλίη, the house 'wanton folly' (the dative of cause). ἀεικέα is the accusative singular of ἀεικής with the ending -έα for -έ(σ)α, agreeing with πότμον, and the house renders the two together as 'an unseemly doom'. ἐπέσπον is the aorist of ἐφέπω 'follow after, meet with'; the suitors ran into their doom.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μετὰ τοῖσι θυοσκόος οὐδὲν ἐοργὼς
κείσομαι, ὡς οὐκ ἔστι χάρις μετόπισθ’ εὐεργέων·
sentences.l:
but I, among them the sacrificing-priest, having done nothing,
shall lie, thus there is no thanks hereafter for the well-doers.”
sentences.i: But I, who was their sacrificing priest and did no wrong, shall lie dead among them: so there is no thanks hereafter for those who do well.”
sentences.n: This is the end of Leiodes’s speech. θυοσκόος is a rare word whose exact function is not certain, one who attends the sacrifices; the house has 'sacrificing priest'. μετὰ τοῖσι is 'among them', and ἐοργώς the perfect participle of ἔρδω (= ῥέζω) 'do', so οὐδὲν ἐοργώς is 'having done nothing', and in his plea that means nothing wrong; the English of the short layer says so. κείσομαι is the future of κεῖμαι 'lie', here 'lie dead'. ὡς οὐκ ἔστι is 'so there is not' (ὡς 'how, so'), and χάρις is 'thanks, gratitude'; εὐεργέων is the genitive plural 'of the well-doers'. The ano teleia after εὐεργέων closes the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. This is the formula for a speech that answers with anger. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is 'looking from under (the brows)', that is 'with a scowl'; τὸν is the article as pronoun, 'him', and προσέφη 'addressed'. πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is the house epithet of Odysseus, translated every time.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ μετὰ τοῖσι θυοσκόος εὔχεαι εἶναι,
πολλάκι που μέλλεις ἀρήμεναι ἐν μεγάροισι
τηλοῦ ἐμοὶ νόστοιο τέλος γλυκεροῖο γενέσθαι,
σοὶ δ’ ἄλοχόν τε φίλην σπέσθαι καὶ τέκνα τεκέσθαι·
sentences.l:
“If indeed among them you declare yourself to be sacrificing-priest,
many times, I suppose, you must have prayed in the halls
far from me that the fulfilment of sweet homecoming should be,
and that my dear wife follow you and bear children;
sentences.i: “If you really claim to be their sacrificing priest, you must often have prayed, I suppose, in these halls that the fulfilment of a sweet homecoming should be far from me, and that my dear wife should follow you and bear children;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks, turning Leiodes’s own claim against him. εἰ μὲν δὴ is 'if indeed', and εὔχεαι is the second person singular of εὔχομαι 'declare, claim', with the old ending -εαι. The main clause is μέλλεις ἀρήμεναι 'you are likely to have prayed'; ἀρήμεναι is the infinitive of ἀράομαι 'pray' in the epic ending -μεναι, and πολλάκι που is 'many times, I suppose'. The infinitives that follow say what he prayed for: τέλος νόστοιο γλυκεροῖο γενέσθαι 'that the fulfilment of a sweet homecoming should come to be', with τηλοῦ ἐμοί 'far from me'; σπέσθαι, the aorist infinitive of ἕπομαι 'follow', which takes the dative σοί 'you' as the man she follows. ἄλοχον φίλην is 'the dear wife', Odysseus’s own wife, so 'my dear wife': the prayer would hand her to Leiodes, and she is the subject of both σπέσθαι and τεκέσθαι. Do not read σοί as 'for yourself' and ἄλοχον as Leiodes’s wife. τεκέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of τίκτω, said of a woman 'bear'. The ano teleia after τεκέσθαι ends the unit.

sentences.t: τῷ οὐκ ἂν θάνατόν γε δυσηλεγέα προφύγοισθα.
sentences.l: Therefore not a painful death, at least, would you escape.”
sentences.i: So you will not escape a painful death.”
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore', as in 317. οὐκ ἂν ... προφύγοισθα is 'you would not escape': ἄν with the optative, the aorist optative of προφεύγω 'escape' in the second person ending -σθα; the effect is a flat refusal. γε 'at least' leans on θάνατον. δυσηλεγέα is an uncertain word: it is taken as 'painful', from δυσ- 'ill' and the root of ἄλγος 'pain', but a derivation from ἀλέγω 'heed' would give 'pitiless'; the sense is not certain. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ξίφος εἵλετο χειρὶ παχείῃ
κείμενον, ὅ ῥ’ Ἀγέλαος ἀποπροέηκε χαμᾶζε
κτεινόμενος·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and took in his stout hand the sword that lay there, which Agelaus had let fall to the ground as he was being killed;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. The subject, Odysseus, is not named. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is 'so then having spoken', and εἵλετο the aorist middle of αἱρέω 'take'. χειρὶ παχείῃ is 'with his thick hand', παχείῃ being the epic feminine of παχύς. κείμενον 'lying' agrees with ξίφος, and ὅ ῥ’ is ὃ ῥα 'which'. ἀποπροέηκε is the aorist of ἀποπροΐημι 'let go, drop', and χαμᾶζε 'to the ground' has the suffix -ζε of direction. κτεινόμενος is the present participle 'as he was being killed': Agelaus dropped it when Odysseus stabbed him at 293. The ano teleia after it closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ τόν γε κατ’ αὐχένα μέσσον ἔλασσε.
sentences.l: with it him indeed on the neck, in the middle, he struck.
sentences.i: With it he struck him in the middle of the neck.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'with it', the sword, a dative of instrument, and not the τῷ 'therefore' of 317. τόν γε is 'him', Leiodes. κατ’ αὐχένα μέσσον is 'on the middle of the neck', with κατά and the accusative of the place struck, and ἔλασσε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'strike', as at 295.

sentences.t: φθεγγομένου δ’ ἄρα τοῦ γε κάρη κονίῃσιν ἐμίχθη.
sentences.l: And as he was speaking, then, his head in the dust was mingled.
sentences.i: As he was speaking, his head was mingled with the dust.
sentences.n: φθεγγομένου τοῦ γε is a genitive absolute, 'he speaking': Leiodes is still speaking as the blow falls. κάρη is 'head', a neuter nominative, and κονίῃσιν the dative plural of κονία 'dust', a plural used for the one dust. ἐμίχθη is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι 'mix', 'was mingled'; the Greek says 'mingled', not 'rolled'.

sentences.t:
Τερπιάδης δ’ ἔτ’ ἀοιδὸς ἀλύσκανε κῆρα μέλαιναν,
Φήμιος, ὅς ῥ’ ἤειδε μετὰ μνηστῆρσιν ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
And Terpes’ son, the minstrel, still was shunning black death-fate,
Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
sentences.i: But the minstrel, son of Terpes, was still trying to keep clear of the black spirit of death, Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Τερπιάδης is the patronymic 'son of Terpes', used as a name for the singer, who is named in the next line. ἀλύσκανε is the imperfect of ἀλυσκάνω, a lengthened form of ἀλύσκω 'shun, keep clear of', and has no augment: 'was trying to keep clear'. κῆρα μέλαιναν is the house 'black death-fate' in the long layer and 'the black spirit of death' in the short; κήρ is a power of death, not death itself. ὅς ῥ’ ἤειδε is 'who sang', the imperfect of ἀείδω, and ἀνάγκῃ the dative 'by compulsion', as of Phemius’s singing at the suitors’ feasts earlier in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἔστη δ’ ἐν χείρεσσίν ἔχων φόρμιγγα λίγειαν
ἄγχι παρ’ ὀρσοθύρην·
sentences.l:
And he stood, in his hands holding the clear-sounding lyre,
close beside the raised door;
sentences.i: He stood with the clear-sounding lyre in his hands, close beside the raised door;
sentences.n: ἔστη is the aorist of ἵστημι in the intransitive sense 'stood'. ἐν χείρεσσιν has the dative plural in -εσσιν, and φόρμιγγα λίγειαν is 'the clear-sounding lyre', the house phrase. ἄγχι παρ’ is 'close beside'. ὀρσοθύρη is the raised door of 22.126 and 22.132, the word being of uncertain sense (what kind of opening it was is not known). The ano teleia after ὀρσοθύρην closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
δίχα δὲ φρεσὶ μερμήριζεν,
ἢ ἐκδὺς μεγάροιο Διὸς μεγάλου ποτὶ βωμὸν
ἑρκείου ἵζοιτο τετυγμένον, ἔνθ’ ἄρα πολλὰ
Λαέρτης Ὀδυσεύς τε βοῶν ἐπὶ μηρί’ ἔκηαν,
sentences.l:
and in two ways in his mind he pondered,
whether, slipping out of the hall, to the altar of great Zeus,
of the courtyard, he should sit, the wrought one, where then many
Laertes and Odysseus of oxen upon it thigh-pieces had burned,
sentences.i: and he was divided in his mind, wondering whether to slip out of the hall and sit at the well-wrought altar of great Zeus of the courtyard, where Laertes and Odysseus had burned many thigh-pieces of oxen,
sentences.n: δίχα ... μερμήριζεν is 'was pondering in two ways', that is 'was torn': μερμηρίζω is 'ponder', δίχα 'in two'. The two choices are ἢ ... ἦ (the second, printed with a circumflex, is also 'or'; see 337). ἐκδύς is the aorist participle of ἐκδύω in the intransitive sense 'slipping out', and ποτὶ βωμόν is πρὸς βωμόν 'to the altar'. ἑρκείου is the genitive of ἑρκεῖος, the adjective from ἕρκος 'fence, enclosure', so the altar is that of 'Zeus of the courtyard', the god of the household’s enclosure; the altar stands in the courtyard (see 376 and 379). ἵζοιτο is the optative of ἵζω 'sit', in a deliberative question, 'whether he should sit'. τετυγμένον is 'well-wrought', and ἐπὶ ... ἔκηαν is tmesis for ἐπέκηαν, the aorist of a verb 'burn upon', with μηρία, the thigh-pieces burned for the gods.

sentences.t: ἦ γούνων λίσσοιτο προσαΐξας Ὀδυσῆα.
sentences.l: or at the knees he should entreat, rushing at Odysseus.
sentences.i: or rush at Odysseus and entreat him at the knees.
sentences.n: ἦ here is ἤ 'or', the second of the two choices begun at 334, not the ἦ of 'so he said'. λίσσοιτο is the optative of λίσσομαι 'entreat', still the deliberative of the question, and γούνων is the genitive 'at the knees', the thing he would grasp. προσαΐξας is the aorist participle of προσαΐσσω 'rush at', and Ὀδυσῆα is its object.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι,
γούνων ἅψασθαι Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be:
the knees to touch of Laertes’ son Odysseus.
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: to clasp the knees of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for a decision, and keeps its English wherever it comes. ὧδε is 'thus', φρονέοντι the dative participle 'considering' agreeing with οἱ 'to him', and δοάσσατο the aorist of an old verb meaning 'seem'. κέρδιον is the comparative 'better, more advantageous'. The infinitive γούνων ἅψασθαι is what seemed best: ἅψασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἅπτω 'touch, take hold of', with the genitive. Λαερτιάδεω is the Ionic genitive of Λαερτιάδης 'son of Laertes'.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ φόρμιγγα γλαφυρὴν κατέθηκε χαμᾶζε
μεσσηγὺς κρητῆρος ἰδὲ θρόνου ἀργυροήλου,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα προσαΐξας λάβε γούνων,
καί μιν λισσόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
Indeed he the hollow lyre set down on the ground
between the mixing-bowl and the silver-studded chair,
and he himself in turn, rushing at Odysseus, took hold of the knees,
and him, entreating, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: He set the hollow lyre down on the ground between the mixing-bowl and the silver-studded chair, and then himself rushed at Odysseus, took hold of his knees, and, entreating him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: The unit is one sentence of four lines. ἦ τοι ὁ is 'truly he', with the article as pronoun, and φόρμιγγα γλαφυρήν is 'the hollow lyre'. κατέθηκε is 'set down', χαμᾶζε 'to the ground', and μεσσηγύς 'between' takes the genitives κρητῆρος 'mixing-bowl' and θρόνου ἀργυροήλου 'silver-studded chair'; ἰδέ is 'and'. αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ is 'and he himself, in his turn', and the last two lines are the formula of 310–311, giving the second choice of 337 in action.

sentences.t: γουνοῦμαί σ’, Ὀδυσεῦ·
sentences.l: “I beseech you at your knees, Odysseus;
sentences.i: “I entreat you, Odysseus;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Phemius speaks, and his first line is word for word line 312, which Leiodes used. The same English follows; see the note there. The ano teleia closes a very short unit.

sentences.t: σὺ δέ μ’ αἴδεο καί μ’ ἐλέησον·
sentences.l: and you, revere me, and pity me;
sentences.i: and you, show me respect and take pity on me;
sentences.n: The second half of the line Leiodes used at 312, with the same words and the same English: αἴδεο is the imperative of αἰδέομαι 'show respect to', and ἐλέησον the aorist imperative of ἐλεέω 'pity'.

sentences.t:
αὐτῷ τοι μετόπισθ’ ἄχος ἔσσεται, εἴ κεν ἀοιδὸν
πέφνῃς, ὅς τε θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ἀείδω.
sentences.l:
To yourself, mark you, afterwards grief will be, if a minstrel
you slay, who for gods and for men I sing.
sentences.i: You will feel grief for it yourself afterwards, if you kill a minstrel, one who sings for gods and for men.
sentences.n: αὐτῷ τοι is 'to yourself, mark you', τοι being a particle of address. ἄχος ἔσσεται is 'there will be grief', ἔσσεται being the future ἔσται with doubled σ. εἴ κεν ... πέφνῃς is 'if you kill', the aorist subjunctive of φένω (stem πεφν-) after εἰ κεν. In ὅς τε ... ἀείδω the verb is in the first person, 'I sing': the relative clause belongs to the minstrel, and the minstrel is the speaker himself; the English keeps 'one who sings'. θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν are the datives in -οισι and -οισιν, 'for gods and for men'.

sentences.t:
αὐτοδίδακτος δ’ εἰμί, θεὸς δέ μοι ἐν φρεσὶν οἴμας
παντοίας ἐνέφυσεν·
sentences.l:
Self-taught I am, and a god in my wits lays
of every kind implanted;
sentences.i: I am self-taught, and a god has implanted in my mind lays of every kind;
sentences.n: αὐτοδίδακτος is 'self-taught' (αὐτός 'self' and διδακτός 'taught'). θεός is 'a god', not named. ἐν φρεσίν is 'in my mind', and οἴμας παντοίας 'lays of every kind', οἴμη being the house 'lay', also 'path of song'. ἐνέφυσεν is the aorist of ἐμφύω in the causative sense 'make grow in, implant'. The ano teleia after it closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἔοικα δέ τοι παραείδειν
ὥς τε θεῷ·
sentences.l:
and I am fit, to you, to sing beside,
as to a god;
sentences.i: and I am fit to sing before you as before a god;
sentences.n: ἔοικα is 'I am fit, it befits me', with the infinitive παραείδειν, and τοι is 'to you'. παραείδειν is παρα- 'beside' with ἀείδειν 'sing', a rare compound: 'sing beside' or 'sing in the presence of' is taken from its parts and its context, and its exact sense is not certain. ὥς τε θεῷ is 'as to a god', with epic τε. The ano teleia after θεῷ closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ μή με λιλαίεο δειροτομῆσαι.
sentences.l: Therefore do not me long to cut-the-throat.
sentences.i: So do not be eager to cut my throat.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore'. μή with λιλαίεο is a prohibition: λιλαίεο is the present imperative of λιλαίομαι 'long for, be eager', with the ending -εο, and it takes the infinitive δειροτομῆσαι 'to cut the throat' (δειρή 'neck, throat' and τέμνω 'cut'), with με as its object.

sentences.t:
καί κεν Τηλέμαχος τάδε γ’ εἴποι, σὸς φίλος υἱός,
ὡς ἐγὼ οὔ τι ἑκὼν ἐς σὸν δόμον οὐδὲ χατίζων
πωλεύμην μνηστῆρσιν ἀεισόμενος μετὰ δαῖτας,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πλέονες καὶ κρείσσονες ἦγον ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
Even Telemachus this at least could say, your dear son,
that I, not at all willing, to your house, nor in need,
kept coming to the suitors, about to sing, to the feasts,
but many more and stronger led me, under compulsion.”
sentences.i: Telemachus too, your dear son, could tell you this: that it was not willingly, nor out of need, that I kept coming to your house to sing to the suitors at their feasts, but that many more and stronger men brought me under compulsion.”
sentences.n: This is the end of Phemius’s plea. καί κεν ... εἴποι is 'could also say', a potential optative, and τάδε γε 'this, at least'; σὸς φίλος υἱός is 'your dear son'. ὡς introduces what Telemachus could say, 'that'. οὔ τι ἑκών is 'not at all willing', and χατίζων 'in need' (χατίζω 'want, need'). πωλεύμην is the imperfect of πωλέομαι 'go regularly to, keep coming', and ἀεισόμενος the future participle of ἀείδω, 'in order to sing'. μετὰ δαῖτας is 'to the feasts'. ἦγον is 'were leading, brought', and ἀνάγκῃ 'under compulsion', as at 331.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο,
αἶψα δ’ ἑὸν πατέρα προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and him heard the sacred force of Telemachus,
and at once to his own father spoke, who was near:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus heard him, and at once spoke to his own father, who was near him:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσ’ is 'and him heard', ἀκούω taking the genitive of the person heard. ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, literally 'the sacred force of Telemachus', is the periphrasis for Telemachus himself, rendered in the house way. ἑὸν πατέρα is 'his own father', ἑός being the possessive 'his own', not the relative. προσεφώνεεν is the imperfect of προσφωνέω 'speak to', in the uncontracted form, and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα is 'who was near'. The ano teleia after it introduces the speech.

sentences.t: ἴσχεο μηδέ τι τοῦτον ἀναίτιον οὔταε χαλκῷ·
sentences.l: “Hold yourself back, and not at all this man, blameless, strike with the bronze;
sentences.i: “Hold back, and do not strike this man, who is blameless, with the bronze;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Telemachus speaks. ἴσχεο is the imperative of ἴσχω in the middle, 'hold yourself back', and μηδέ τι is 'and not at all'. τοῦτον is Phemius, and ἀναίτιον 'blameless' is the negative of αἴτιος 'to blame': a man free of fault, not the ἀμύμων of the stock epithet. οὔταε is the second person singular imperative of οὐτάω 'wound by a thrust' in its uncontracted epic form (Attic οὔτα); μηδέ gives it the force of a prohibition. χαλκῷ 'with the bronze' is the weapon.

sentences.t:
καὶ κήρυκα Μέδοντα σαώσομεν, ὅς τέ μευ αἰεὶ
οἴκῳ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ κηδέσκετο παιδὸς ἐόντος,
εἰ δὴ μή μιν ἔπεφνε Φιλοίτιος ἠὲ συβώτης,
ἠὲ σοὶ ἀντεβόλησεν ὀρινομένῳ κατὰ δῶμα.
sentences.l:
and the herald Medon let us save, who always
in our house cared for me when I was a child,
unless indeed him Philoetius has killed, or the swineherd,
or he has met you, stirred up, through the house.”
sentences.i: and let us save the herald Medon too, who always looked after me in our house when I was a boy, unless Philoetius or the swineherd has killed him, or he has met you in your fury as you went through the house.”
sentences.n: This is the end of Telemachus’s speech. σαώσομεν may be a future ('we shall save') or a short-vowel subjunctive ('let us save'); the sense of an urgent request is 'let us save'. ὅς τέ μευ αἰεὶ is 'who always ... me', μευ being the genitive of ἐγώ, and κηδέσκετο the iterative imperfect of κήδομαι 'care for', which takes μευ in the genitive. παιδὸς ἐόντος is a genitive phrase agreeing with μευ, 'I being a child', not a genitive absolute. εἰ δὴ μή is 'unless indeed', followed by two alternatives with ἠέ ... ἠέ: Philoetius or the swineherd 'has killed' him (ἔπεφνε, the aorist of φένω), or he 'has met' you (ἀντεβόλησεν, with the dative σοί), 'as you were stirred up' (ὀρινομένῳ, the passive participle of ὀρίνω). Φιλοίτιος is the cowherd and συβώτης the swineherd.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσε Μέδων πεπνυμένα εἰδώς·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him heard Medon, prudent counsels knowing;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Medon, a man versed in prudent counsels, heard him;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Medon is the herald Telemachus has just named. τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσε is 'and him heard', with the genitive of the person heard, as at 354. πεπνυμένα εἰδώς is Medon’s standing description, 'knowing prudent things': πεπνυμένα is the neuter plural of πεπνυμένος 'prudent', and εἰδώς the perfect participle of οἶδα. The ano teleia introduces the explanation in the next lines.

sentences.t:
πεπτηὼς γὰρ ἔκειτο ὑπὸ θρόνον, ἀμφὶ δὲ δέρμα
ἕστο βοὸς νεόδαρτον, ἀλύσκων κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.l:
for crouching he lay beneath a chair, and about him a hide
of an ox he was clad in, newly flayed, shunning black death-fate.
sentences.i: for he lay crouching under a chair, clad in the hide of an ox, freshly flayed, and keeping clear of the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: γάρ 'for' explains the scene: where Medon was when he heard. πεπτηώς is the perfect participle of πτήσσω 'crouch, cower', and ἔκειτο 'he lay'; the accusative after ὑπό suggests motion into the place, 'he had got under a chair'. ἀμφὶ ... ἕστο is tmesis for ἀμφίεστο, the pluperfect middle of ἀμφιέννυμι, 'was clothed in'. δέρμα βοὸς νεόδαρτον is 'an ox’s hide, newly flayed' (νεόδαρτος from νέος and δέρω 'flay'). ἀλύσκων is the participle of ἀλύσκω, the verb of 330; κῆρα μέλαιναν keeps its house English.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἀπὸ θρόνου ὦρτο, θοῶς δ’ ἀπέδυνε βοείην·
sentences.l: And at once from the chair he sprang up, and quickly he stripped off the oxhide;
sentences.i: At once he sprang up from the chair and quickly threw off the oxhide;
sentences.n: ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι 'sprang up'. ἀπέδυνε is the imperfect of ἀποδύνω, a by-form of ἀποδύω 'strip off', used of taking off the hide, and βοείην is 'oxhide', the adjective βοείη used as a noun for δέρμα βοός of the line before. The ano teleia closes the first movement; the suppliant’s approach follows.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα προσαΐξας λάβε γούνων,
καί μιν λισσόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and Telemachus then, rushing at him, he took hold of by the knees,
and him, entreating, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: then he rushed at Telemachus, took hold of his knees, and, entreating him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Τηλέμαχον ... λάβε γούνων has both an accusative of the person and a genitive of the part taken: 'he took Telemachus by the knees', the suppliant’s gesture for the third time (310, 342). The last line is the formula of 311 and 343.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐγὼ μὲν ὅδ’ εἰμί, σὺ δ’ ἴσχεο, εἰπὲ δὲ πατρὶ
μή με περισθενέων δηλήσεται ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων κεχολωμένος, οἵ οἱ ἔκειρον
κτήματ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροις, σὲ δὲ νήπιοι οὐδὲν ἔτιον.
sentences.l:
“O friend, I indeed am here, and you restrain yourself, and tell your father
not to harm me, being very strong, with sharp bronze,
angered at the men, the suitors, who for him were stripping away
possessions in the halls, and you, the fools, in nothing honoured.”
sentences.i: “Friend, here I am; hold back, and tell your father not to harm me with sharp bronze, strong as he is, in his anger at the suitors who stripped away his possessions in the halls and, fools that they were, gave you no honour at all.”
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Medon speaks, and the whole speech is one sentence. ὦ φίλ’ is 'friend', and ἐγὼ μὲν ὅδ’ εἰμί 'here I am', ὅδε pointing to himself. σὺ δ’ ἴσχεο εἰπὲ δὲ πατρί runs two imperatives together, 'you, hold back, and tell your father'. μή με ... δηλήσεται is 'that he may not harm me', μή with the future of δηλέομαι 'harm'. περισθενέων is 'being exceedingly strong', and κεχολωμένος the perfect participle of χολόω, 'angered', with the genitive ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων. οἵ οἱ ἔκειρον is 'who ... for him were stripping', οἵ the relative 'who' and οἱ 'for him', ἔκειρον being the imperfect of κείρω 'shear', that is 'strip bare', and κτήματα 'possessions'. νήπιοι is 'fools', and ἔτιον the imperfect of τίω 'honour'; σὲ οὐδὲν ἔτιον is 'did not honour you at all'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then smiling at addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, smiling at him, spoke to him:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. This is the formula for a speech answering a plea, as ὑπόδρα ἰδών was for Leiodes’s. ἐπιμειδήσας is the aorist participle of ἐπιμειδάω 'smile at', and it is the opposite of the scowl: Medon has nothing to fear. τὸν is the article as pronoun, 'him', and προσέφη 'addressed'.

sentences.t:
θάρσει, ἐπεὶ δή σ’ οὗτος ἐρύσσατο καὶ ἐσάωσεν,
ὄφρα γνῷς κατὰ θυμόν, ἀτὰρ εἴπῃσθα καὶ ἄλλῳ,
ὡς κακοεργίης εὐεργεσίη μέγ’ ἀμείνων.
sentences.i: “Take courage, since this man has rescued you and saved you, so that you may know it in your heart and tell another too how much better doing good is than doing evil;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω 'take courage'. οὗτος is 'this man', Telemachus, who stands there. ἐρύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι 'rescue, protect', and ἐσάωσεν the aorist of σαόω 'save'. ὄφρα γνῷς is ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω 'know', 'so that you may know', and εἴπῃσθα the aorist subjunctive of εἶπον with the second person ending -σθα, 'and tell'. In ὡς κακοεργίης εὐεργεσίη μέγ’ ἀμείνων the genitive κακοεργίης is the genitive of comparison, 'than evil-doing'; εὐεργεσίη is 'well-doing', the doing of good, and μέγ’ ἀμείνων is 'much better'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐξελθόντες μεγάρων ἕζεσθε θύραζε
ἐκ φόνου εἰς αὐλήν, σύ τε καὶ πολύφημος ἀοιδός,
ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ κατὰ δῶμα πονήσομαι ὅττεό με χρή.
sentences.l:
but, having gone out of the halls, sit down outside,
out of the slaughter into the courtyard, you and the many-voiced minstrel,
while I through the house shall toil at whatever is needful for me.”
sentences.i: Now go out of the halls and sit outside, out of the slaughter and into the courtyard, you and the many-voiced minstrel, while I go through the house and do the work I must.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is 'but, now then', turning from the maxim to the order. ἐξελθόντες is the aorist participle 'having gone out', addressed to both men, and ἕζεσθε the imperative of ἕζομαι 'sit down', θύραζε 'outside' with the suffix -ζε. ἐκ φόνου εἰς αὐλήν is 'out of the slaughter into the courtyard' (φόνος 'slaughter', αὐλή 'courtyard'). πολύφημος is of uncertain sense: 'of many voices', for a singer, or 'much spoken of'; the house takes the first without ruling out the second. ὄφρ’ ἂν ... πονήσομαι is ὄφρα ἄν with a form that may be the future or a short-vowel subjunctive, 'while I labour'. ὅττεό με χρή is 'of what there is need to me', that is 'whatever I need to do'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὼ δ’ ἔξω βήτην μεγάροιο κιόντε,
ἑζέσθην δ’ ἄρα τώ γε Διὸς μεγάλου ποτὶ βωμόν,
πάντοσε παπταίνοντε, φόνον ποτιδεγμένω αἰεί.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and the two outside went out of the hall, going,
and sat down, then, those two, by the altar of great Zeus,
glancing everywhere, slaughter expecting always.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the two of them went out of the hall and sat down by the altar of great Zeus, glancing about on every side, always expecting slaughter.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. The verbs and participles are in the dual, for the two men: τὼ δ’ 'and the two', βήτην 'they went' (the dual aorist of βαίνω), κιόντε 'going', ἑζέσθην 'they sat down' (the dual aorist of ἕζομαι), τώ γε 'those two', παπταίνοντε 'glancing about', and ποτιδεγμένω 'expecting' (the dual of ποτιδέγμενος, an old participle of ποτιδέχομαι with present force). ποτὶ βωμόν is πρὸς βωμόν 'to the altar', the altar of 334–336. φόνον is 'slaughter', as in ἐκ φόνου.

sentences.t:
πάπτηνεν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καθ’ ἑὸν δόμον, εἴ τις ἔτ’ ἀνδρῶν
ζωὸς ὑποκλοπέοιτο, ἀλύσκων κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.l:
And he peered about, Odysseus, through his own house, whether any still of men
alive was hiding away, shunning black death-fate.
sentences.i: Odysseus looked all through his house, to see whether any man was still alive and hiding, keeping clear of the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: πάπτηνεν is the aorist of παπταίνω 'look about', and καθ’ ἑὸν δόμον is 'through his own house', ἑός being the possessive. εἴ τις ἔτ’ ἀνδρῶν is 'if any of the men still', the suitors. ὑποκλοπέοιτο is the optative of ὑποκλοπέομαι, a rare verb whose sense, 'steal away under cover, lie hidden', is taken from κλέπτω 'steal' and from the context. The optative is that of an indirect question after a past tense. ἀλύσκων κῆρα μέλαιναν is the phrase of 330 and 363.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἴδεν μάλα πάντας ἐν αἵματι καὶ κονίῃσι
πεπτεῶτας πολλούς, ὥστ’ ἰχθύας, οὕς θ’ ἁλιῆες
κοῖλον ἐς αἰγιαλὸν πολιῆς ἔκτοσθε θαλάσσης
δικτύῳ ἐξέρυσαν πολυωπῷ·
sentences.l:
And them he saw, quite all, in blood and in dust
fallen, many, like fishes, which the fishermen
onto the hollow shore, out of the grey sea,
with a net have drawn out, many-meshed;
sentences.i: He saw them all lying fallen in blood and dust, in great numbers, like fishes which fishermen have drawn out of the grey sea onto the hollow shore with a many-meshed net;
sentences.n: A second simile follows the first. τοὺς is 'them', the suitors, and ἴδεν the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω. μάλα πάντας is 'every one'. πεπτεῶτας is the perfect participle of πίπτω in the Ionic form (Attic πεπτωκότας), 'fallen', and κονίῃσι the dative plural of κονία 'dust'. ὥστ’ is ὥς τε 'like', ἰχθύας the accusative plural of ἰχθύς 'fish', and οὕς θ’ 'which', with epic τε. ἁλιῆες are 'fishermen', and κοῖλον αἰγιαλόν 'the hollow shore', a curving beach; πολιῆς ... θαλάσσης is 'the grey sea', and ἔκτοσθε 'out of' takes its genitive. ἐξέρυσαν is the aorist of ἐξερύω 'draw out', here in a general simile. δικτύῳ ... πολυωπῷ is 'with a many-meshed net': πολυωπός is rare, and the sense, 'with many openings', is taken from ὀπή 'opening'; it might also be 'many-eyed', and the exact sense is not certain. The ano teleia after πολυωπῷ closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ τε πάντες
κύμαθ’ ἁλὸς ποθέοντες ἐπὶ ψαμάθοισι κέχυνται·
sentences.l:
and these all
the waves of the salt-sea longing for, on the sands lie poured out;
sentences.i: and every one of them lies scattered on the sand, longing for the waves of the salt sea;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ τε πάντες is 'and these all', the fishes, with epic τε. κύμαθ’ is κύματα 'waves', the object of ποθέοντες, the participle of ποθέω 'long for' in the uncontracted form, and ἁλός is the genitive of ἅλς 'salt sea'. ἐπὶ ψαμάθοισι is 'on the sands', the dative plural of ψάμαθος. κέχυνται is the perfect passive of χέω 'pour', 'have been poured out' and so 'lie scattered'.

sentences.t: τῶν μέν τ’ Ἠέλιος φαέθων ἐξείλετο θυμόν·
sentences.l: and of them the shining Sun has taken out the life;
sentences.i: and the shining Sun takes the life out of them;
sentences.n: τῶν μέν τ’ is 'and of them', with epic τε. Ἠέλιος φαέθων is 'the shining Sun', φαέθων being a participle of φαέθω 'shine' that has become a standing epithet. ἐξείλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω 'take out', in a general sense, so the English may use the present; θυμός here is 'life', the breath that leaves a body. The fish die on the sand under the Sun.

sentences.t: ὣς τότ’ ἄρα μνηστῆρες ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι κέχυντο.
sentences.l: So then the suitors upon one another lay scattered.
sentences.i: So the suitors lay then, scattered upon one another.
sentences.n: ὣς τότ’ ἄρα 'so then' brings the poem back from the simile to the suitors. κέχυντο is the pluperfect passive of χέω, 'lay poured out', without augment, the past of κέχυνται two lines above, and ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι is 'upon one another'.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε Τηλέμαχον προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Then indeed to Telemachus addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles said to Telemachus:
sentences.n: δὴ τότε ... προσέφη is the formula for a speech that does not answer anyone: the speaker begins, so the English has 'said to', not 'answered'. Τηλέμαχον is the accusative of the person addressed, and Ὀδυσσεύς with its epithet the subject; πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is the house epithet.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, εἰ δ’ ἄγε μοι κάλεσον τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν,
ὄφρα ἔπος εἴπωμι τό μοι καταθύμιόν ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, but come, call for me the nurse Eurycleia,
so that a word I may say which to me is in-the-heart.”
sentences.i: “Telemachus, come now, call the nurse Eurycleia for me, so that I may say the word I have on my mind.”
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Odysseus speaks again. Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative, and εἰ δ’ ἄγε is 'but come now'. κάλεσον is the aorist imperative of καλέω 'call', with μοι 'for me', and τροφόν is 'nurse'. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive εἴπωμι (the ending -ωμι for -ω) is 'so that I may say'. καταθύμιον is built on κατά and θυμός, 'in the heart or mind', and τό μοι καταθύμιόν ἐστιν is 'the word that is on my mind'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθετο πατρί,
κινήσας δὲ θύρην προσέφη τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and, having moved the door, addressed the nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father; he pushed at the door and spoke to the nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.n: The first line is a line already published, and keeps its English. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect middle of πείθω 'obey', with the dative φίλῳ ... πατρί. κινήσας is the aorist participle of κινέω 'set in motion': he pushed or rattled the door to call through it, and the Greek does not say which. προσέφη is 'addressed', with τροφόν 'the nurse' as its object. The ano teleia introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
δεῦρο δὴ ὄρσο, γρηῢ παλαιγενές, ἥ τε γυναικῶν
δμῳάων σκοπός ἐσσι κατὰ μέγαρ’ ἡμετεράων·
sentences.l:
“Come here now, rise up, old woman of ancient birth, you who of the women,
the maidservants, are watcher throughout the halls, of ours;
sentences.i: “Come here now, rouse yourself, old woman of great age, you who are the overseer of our maidservants throughout the halls;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Telemachus speaks. δεῦρο δή is 'come here now', and ὄρσο the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι, 'rouse yourself, get up'. γρηῢ is the vocative of γρηῦς 'old woman', and παλαιγενές the vocative of παλαιγενής, 'born long ago', that is of great age. ἥ τε is 'you who', with epic τε. σκοπός is 'watcher', the word that is a 'lookout' at 22.156; here the one who watches over the maidservants. δμῳάων is the genitive plural of δμῳή 'maidservant', and ἡμετεράων 'of ours' agrees with it. ἐσσι is εἶ 'you are', and κατὰ μέγαρ’ 'throughout the halls', with elision.

sentences.t: ἔρχεο· κικλήσκει σε πατὴρ ἐμός, ὄφρα τι εἴπῃ.
sentences.l: Come; he calls you, my father, so that he may say something.”
sentences.i: Come: my father is calling you, so that he may tell you something.”
sentences.n: ἔρχεο is the imperative of ἔρχομαι 'come', here said from the doorway to someone inside; the ano teleia stands after the one word, in mid-line. κικλήσκει is 'calls, summons', the reduplicated present of καλέω, and σε πατὴρ ἐμός is 'my father calls you'. ὄφρα τι εἴπῃ is ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive, 'so that he may say something'. This ends the speech.
